title: Green Sea Turtles Are Making a Comeback
summary:
On a quiet beach at night, a green sea turtle climbs out of the sea to lay her eggs. On Aldabra, a far-off island group 400 miles off Africa's east coast, this sight is much more common than it was 50 years ago.

People once hunted green turtles for meat, leather, and eggs. By the 1960s, only 2,000 to 3,000 nests were found on Aldabra each year. A hunting ban in 1968 gave the turtles safety, and researchers have watched their nests for more than 50 years.

The wait was long because green turtles do not start breeding until they are 25 to 35 years old. But the turtles came back. In 2019, workers counted more than 15,000 groups of eggs, a 173 percent rise since 1980.

In October 2025, the International Union for Conservation of Nature moved green turtles from endangered to least concern. Still, the recovery is not even. One small group in the south-central Pacific is in serious trouble, and environmental economist Adam Pritchard says the work is definitely not done.
why_it_matters: Protecting animals can help them come back, so the beaches and oceans you visit one day may still have sea turtles.
